_source.Title: Enhanced Particle Tracking in STDC Data and Its Industrial Application of Marangoni Convection
_source.Keywords: STDCE     Particle tracking analysis     thermo-fluid mechanics     Marangoni convection
_source.Proposal Title: Enhanced Particle Tracking in STDC Data and Its Industrial Application of Marangoni Convection
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI Grant
_source.Objectives: The primary objective this grant was to extract and understand the detailed thermo-fluid mechanics of the original NASA Surface Tension Driven Convection Experiment (STDCE-1) performed in microgravity, using modern diagnostic and computational tools. The study aims to revitalize the original video data found in PSI by applying advanced Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) methods, which provide higher resolution, sub-pixel accuracy, and robust flow field extraction compared to the limited analyses available in the early 1990s. By systematically comparing velocity and pressure fields obtained from these reanalyzed datasets with theoretical perturbation methods and COMSOL Multiphysics computational models, the project seeks to isolate the fundamental role of Marangoni convection and interfacial curvature in driving oscillatory and steady-state flows. Complementary ground-based experiments incorporating gravitational effects will be conducted to disentangle the relative contributions of buoyancy and surface tension-driven convection. These objectives ultimately support both NASA’s PSI solicitation  by expanding the scientific return from legacy datasets and advancing applied understanding for industrial processes that rely on controlled Marangoni flows, such as wafer drying, thin-film coating, and microfluidic device operation.
_source.Approach: The approach combined archival microgravity data analysis, computational modeling, and ground experiments to study surface tension driven convection (STDC). Video data from the original NASA STDCE-1 experiments were re-analyzed using several modern particle tracking techniques, including four MATLAB-based codes, three ImageJ-based codes, and sub-pixel localization methods, to produce velocity and pressure fields. These flow fields were compared with theoretical models derived from perturbation methods and with computational simulations performed in COMSOL Multiphysics® v5.6 that incorporated boundary conditions and curved free-surface geometries. In parallel, ground-based STDC experiments were carried out to examine gravitational effects and to distinguish buoyancy-driven flows from thermocapillary convection. This combination of data reanalysis, numerical simulation, and experimental testing provided a means to identify the influence of interfacial curvature, surface stresses, and geometry on Marangoni convection.
_source.Hypothesis: Re-analyzing NASA’s STDCE-1 microgravity video data with advanced particle tracking and computational modeling to reveal previously inaccessible details of thermo-fluid mechanics in surface tension driven convection. These insights, validated against ground-based experiments, aimed to clarify the interplay between Marangoni forces, interfacial curvature, and flow instabilities, leading to improved predictive models of thermocapillary flows.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Space Benefits: Improves understanding of thermocapillary convection in microgravity, critical for designing reliable thermal management and materials processing systems aboard spacecraft. Provides validated numerical and theoretical models that can guide future ISS and space-based fluid physics experiments, reducing uncertainty from prior low-resolution analyses.
Earth Benefits: Supports industrial applications such as semiconductor wafer cleaning, thin-film coatings, welding, and liquid crystal display fabrication. Findings also translate to emerging fields like active matter and micro/nano robotics, where Marangoni flows and surface interactions could be harnessed for medical diagnostics, targeted drug delivery, and microplastics removal.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 6
_source.Keywords: Colloid     Polydispersity     Gels and Creams     microgravity
_source.Sponsoring Agency: Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS)
_source.Objectives: ACE-T6 studies the microscopic behavior of colloids in gels and creams.  Consumer products are often required to be ‘structured’ by colloidal gels to prevent instability - or bulk separation of dispersed benefit actives. Benefit actives are generally dispersed as micron-size drops in liquid products to impart a consumer benefit, such as fabric softness. This leads to a fundamental challenge- how do you preventing bulk separation of the actives (i.e. maintain shelf life) while at the same time maintaining the relative ease-of-flow characteristics of the products. The objective of ACE-T6 is to use confocal microscopy to study the 3D behavior of microscopic particles in gels and creams, to advance knowledge of the fundamental physics associated with gel coarsening to improve the shelf-life stability of products. The microgravity environment on ISS was required to detach phase separation from coarsening.
_source.Approach: The ACE-T6 investigation utilized a single Sample Module (SM) having 3 temperature controlled capillary cells with 20 ml colloidal sample fluid and each having differing particle concentration. The capillary cells were situated on the temperature gradient stage (typical range: 20 – 60 °C, 10 °C temperature differential over the full length). The experiment employed confocal microscopy, which uses a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner allowed 30 frames per second of confocal images to be taken by the CCD camera. A sample’s 3D crystal structure was reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program, from which colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics can be observed and measured. To obtain statistically meaningful data, at least ten colloidal structures in each capillary was imaged, for at least ~400 minutes of observation on each capillary.
_source.Hypothesis: ACE-T6 addresses the effect of polydispersity on coarsening in colloidal systems. It is hypothesized that polydispersity in the polymer makes order-of-magnitude differences in the time scale of collapse of weak gels. The investigation attempts to make benchmark microgravity measurements and advance theories that allow a more comprehensive understanding of the role of polydispersity in the coarsening process.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This research will have significant impact in two areas. First, in the scientific community, there is a large disconnect between microscopic structure and dynamics of these mixtures to the macroscopic changes in the structure which lead to collapse. This work will significantly enhance the knowledge necessary to advance this important area of science. Second, understanding this relationship should enable us to anticipate instability in products, directly impacting the development of multi-billion dollar products and initiatives which improve the lives of 4.8 billion people on Earth per day from products originating from Procter and Gamble alone. Understanding the behavior of mixtures and coarsening can help materials scientists to make colloidal mixtures with longer shelf lives. This has great potentials in creating a wide range of products from food, medicine, cosmetics, gels, and cleaning solutions which do not expire quickly.

_source.Title: Advanced Colloids Experiment - Temperature 1
_source.Keywords: Colloid     Janus particle     Self assembly     microgravity
_source.Objectives: The ACE-T1 investigation seeks to answer fundamental questions about behaviors of colloids, helping scientists to understand how to control, change, and even reverse interactions between tiny particles.  The objective is to build a fundamental understanding of the behavior of antisotropic (directionally dependent) Janus particles and their 3D self-assembly in microgravity. For decades, important advances have been reported in the literature regarding the effects of directionally dependent particles, both the chemical and morphological aspects, that provide the potential to extend the complexity of the self-assembled structures.
_source.Approach: The ACE-T1 investigation was executed in 2 phases and utilized 3 Sample Modules (SM), each having 3 temperature controlled capillary cells with 20 ml sample fluid each. Phase 2 was a re-run of the T1-103 SM and employed confocal microscopy, which uses a 532-nm frequency-doubled Nd:YAG laser, a confocal scanner, and an 8- to 12-bit digital CCD camera. The scanner allowed 30 frames per second of confocal images to be taken by the CCD camera. A sample’s 3D crystal structure was reconstructed by assembling individual slices with an image analysis program, from which colloidal growth, structure, and dynamics can be observed and measured. To obtain statistically meaningful data, at least ten colloidal structures in one capillary cell was imaged, at least ~400 minutes of observation on each capillary.
_source.Hypothesis: Fundamental science and colloidal engineering can be pursued and understood directly at a particle level. Microscopy enables scientists to directly observe what is happening at a colloid particle level - one no longer requires a theoretical model to hope to connect macroscopic experimental observations to microscopic ones (as when observing experiments at the size scale seen with a photograph taken of a BCAT or PCS sample).
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
SPACE APPLICATIONS
Observing colloidal interactions without the influence of gravity provides new insight into how unhindered particles form network and structures. Results from ACE-T1 lay a foundation for understanding this mechanism. Very small scale self-assembly of materials can be an efficient method to build new materials and equipment in space.
EARTH APPLICATIONS
The ACE-T1 investigation seeks to answer fundamental questions about behaviors of colloids, helping scientists to understand how to control, change, and even reverse interactions between tiny particles. This knowledge is crucial for developing self-assembling, self-moving, and self-replicating technologies for use on Earth. It is anticipated that this novel fabrication approach can be applied to produce novel functional material in various applications such as self-assembly, photonics, diagnostics, and drug-delivery.

_source.Title: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
_source.Keywords: Cool Flame Transitions     Ground-based experiments     Flames     Radiation     Low temperature flames     Counterflow flames     Extinction Limit     n-alkane     FLEX     Dibutyl Ether     Modeling     Kinetic experiments     Emissions     Supercritical Reacting Fluids     Low temperature chemistry     PSI Grant
_source.Objectives:
By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
    1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
    2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
    3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
    4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.
    5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.
_source.Approach:
Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures.

Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

_source.Title: Colloidal gels:  Aging in microgravity, Structure of highly polydisperse gels
_source.Keywords: colloids     microgravity     fractal     gels     experiment     polydisperse
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI Grant
_source.Objectives:
Data are from two projects:  one related to aging, one related to polydispersity.  The first project has data under folders with a name containing AGING.  The second has data under folders with a name containing POLYDISPERSE.

-------

Project 1: Objectives specific to aging of colloid gels
•Quantify coarsening of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions.
•Quantify changes in thermal fluctuations of colloidal gels under microgravity conditions.
•Understand aging of colloidal gels over time scales range from seconds to tens of hours.

Project 2: Objectives related to structure of polydisperse colloidal gels
•Measure fractal dimension of polydisperse colloidal gels (on Earth)
•Understand how particle size relates to contact number
•Quantify tetrahedral structures, and how particle size influences tetrahedral structure in colloidal gels
_source.Approach:
Project 1: We studied colloidal gels using the data from the Advanced Colloids Experiment-Microscopy-1 (ACE-M1) experiments. Colloidal gels are formed from sticky micron-sized solid particles in a liquid, where over time the particles stick together and form random clumps that eventually bridge across the entire sample chamber in tangled networks. The ACE-M1 data set consists of a large number of optical microscopy movies of colloidal gels. In microgravity, these gels are long-lived, rather than collapsing under their own weight as happens in ground-based experiments. We have analyzed these microscopy movies using particle tracking, studying the visible thermal fluctuations and the gel structure as it evolves over time. Some gels have thick aggregated regions, while others have more tenuous gel strands and free particles. We show that the structure and dynamics change over the several-day period of each experiment.

Project 2: In a second project, we did ground-based experiments to study the structure of colloidal gels composed of polydisperse particles.  In particular, we used confocal microscopy to image colloidal gels formed from highly polydisperse particles. We suspended our polydisperse particles in a density matched solvent, and let the particles spontaneously aggregate through the van der Waals force. The largest particles were more than 15 times the size of the smallest particles.  As expected, larger particles have more nearest neighbors than small ones.  This leads to an over-representation of large particles in tetrahedral structures where four particles are mutually nearest neighbors, showing that large particles help provide rigidity to the gel structure.  The tetrahedral structures also suggest that particles are able to rearrange somewhat during the gelation process, until their motion is stabilized by the multiple contacts with their neighbors.
_source.Hypothesis:
Project 1:  Colloidal gels in microgravity conditions will coarsen over time, and their thermal fluctuations will diminish over time as the gel gets coarser; the coarsening will continue indefinitely because gravitational collapse will not be possible.

Project 2:  Large particles play significant roles in highly polydisperse colloidal gels, as they serve as highly connected nodes in the structure.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This research helps us understand the technical challenge of keeping particles dispersed in a colloidal suspension.  A gel is one way to prevent particles from settling, although the long-time behavior of a gel is challenging to study under Earth gravity.

_source.Title: Spurious Grain Formation in Alloys Directionally Solidified on the Space Station Due to Marangoni Convection
_source.Keywords: Dendritic solidification     grant     Spurious grain formation     Marangoni convection
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI Grant
_source.Objectives: Develop a three dimensional solidification model incorporating Marangoni convection and thermosolutal convection which can predict formation of spurious grains during DS. Extract data, such as, fluid velocities along stream lines as a function of distance from the surface-void, angular rotation of the fragmented side arms due to Marangoni flow lines, etc. from PFMI (Pore Formation and Mobility Investigation) videos, and then compare these observations with the simulations in order to quantitatively validate our numerical model. Use that model to predict formation of spurious grains in a totally different alloy, Al-7Si (MICAST), under varying processing conditions, such as, during re-melting prior to DS, after a step increase or decrease in growth speed vs at constant speed, etc.
_source.Approach: Use the PFMI and MICAST experimental flight data available in PSI to validate a three dimensional solidification model to predict that formation of spurious grains during DS.
_source.Hypothesis:
Columnar and dendritic growth experiments in a predominantly diffusive microgravity environment have shown the presence of voids at the
melt-crucible interface which are the likely the source of Marangoni convective flows. It is hypothesized that it is this flow that is responsible for fragmentation of the dendrite-side arm, and its rotation which creates the nucleus for the subsequent growth and formation of spurious grains. This hypothesis was tested by numerically simulating the influence of the Marangoni convection on the trajectory of such a dendrite fragment in the alloy melt and comparing with the experimental observations.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Results from this research are valuable not only for terrestrial technologies involving solidification, such as repairing gas turbine blade tips by laser cladding, but also for any future space manufacture or repair which involves solidification.

_source.Keywords: Magnetic Colloids     Magnetic fields     self-assembly     magnetorheological (MR) fluid     nanomaterials     assembly kinetics     anisotropic particle     toggled fields

_source.Objectives: The overall objective of the InSPACE-4 investigation was to study the effects of particle shape and toggle duty cycle on the phase separation kinetics of particles in toggled fields. Three specific objectives include: (1) investigation of phase separation kinetics of anisotropic particles in toggled fields, (2) study the effect of toggle duty-cycle on the phase diagram, and (3) perform concurrent ground-based self-assembly experiments using the same magnetic colloids and extend the work to dielectric (insulating) particles driven by toggled alternating current (AC) electric fields.Concurrent ground-based experiments help translate International Space Station (ISS) discoveries to Earth-based manufacture by providing additional insights into the structure of equilibrated phases.
_source.Approach: This ISS investigation was conducted using  magnetic prolate ellipsoids with aspect ratios ranging from 2:1 to 4:1. Experiments involving spheres was also be conducted for comparison purposes. The sample material consisted of randomly oriented nano Fe3O4 coated polymer beads within a fluid filled vial, creating a magnetorheological fluid (MR). The vials were subjected to a pulsed magnetic field, which created a configuration of three-dimensional structures.The particle orientation was determined from birefringence measurements using crossed polarizers. The effects of particle shape, anisotropy, and magnetic field toggling frequency on the phase separation of particles was examined. Relatively short duration, ground-based experiments was conducted using the same magnetic particles to provide additional details about structure formation from particle-level to mesoscale structure.
_source.Hypothesis: Due to their anisotropic dynamics and interactions, investigators hypothesize that particle shape, in particular anisotropy (having different physical properties along different molecular axes), affects the phase separation kinetics of suspensions in toggled fields. Theoretical and simulation results suggesting that dynamic self-assembly can access a broad range of states analogous to equilibrium phases, even metastable ones, was also tested.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Discoveries from this work could lead to advanced materials for space applications such as better thermal shields, protection from micrometeorites, materials for energy production, energy-transfer devices, control systems and new mechanical actuators and sensors for robotic and human missions. This investigation helps advance the manufacture of next-generation nanomaterials for applications on Earth such as thermal shields, sound damping devices, shock absorbers, camouflage, medical diagnostic and environmental sensors, display technologies and advanced coatings. The technology also is expanding into larger-scale applications such as building foundation stabilizers for areas prone to earthquakes.

_source.Title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
_source.Keywords: BASS     Flamelet Generated Manifolds     Flame Spread
_source.Proposal Title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography
_source.Objectives:
The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.
To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.
_source.Approach:
The approach combined high-resolution computational modeling with experimental validation to study concurrent flame spread in microgravity. A previously developed computational framework  was employed to run fully coupled simulations of fluid–solid responses, focusing on materials subject to charring and ablation. Within this framework, the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders.
Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions. The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.
_source.Hypothesis: The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity, including phenomena such as the “Goldilocks” flammability zone, by coupling near-wall thermal, mass transport, and chemical processes with far-field flow dynamics.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: This research provides predictive tools for screening new materials’ flammability limits, which can lead to the design of safer spacecrafts. The development of Large Eddy Simulation subgrid models is expected to improve hazard assessment capabilities critical for managing fire risks during long-duration space missions and within confined spacecraft habitats. On Earth, these advancements could improve combustion modeling by deepening our understanding of coupled thermal, chemical, and flow processes, which betters fire safety standards. The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies and  foster innovations in diagnostics and simulations applicable across a variety of combustion scenarios. Overall, this research can contribute significantly to safer human exploration in space and improvements to fire safety protocols on Earth.

_source.Objectives: The key objectives of this investigation were to develop 1) a binary Molecular Dynamics (MD) interatomic potential for Pb-Sn system, 2) Phase Field Crystal (PFC) models for coarsening of solid-liquid mixtures; 3) a highly-parallel semi-implicit spectral and operator splitting numerical algorithm to use on high performance computing facilities that will enable the necessary large-scale PFC simulations (comparable to CSLM data length-scale); (4) Data mining of NASA-PSI Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM), CSLM-2, CSLM-2R, and CSLM-3 experiments and using them in series of simulations in the developed computational tool for enhancement and verification of the proposed modeling framework.
_source.Approach:
The proposed multi-scale modeling framework is established around two atomistic computational material model of phase-field crystals (PFC) and molecular dynamics (MD). PFC is a unique computational model at diffusive time scale with the capability of simulating solid-liquid processes with atomistic resolutions while MD acts on the time scale of atomistic vibrations.
A novel approach of modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential was adopted to obtain reliable interatomic potentials for Pb-Sn binary systems near or at the melting point (MP). The potentials were used to calculate relevant properties such as latent heat, expansion in melting, liquid structure factor, solid-liquid interface stiffness, solidus and liquidus lines, and solid-liquid interfacial free energy. The kinetics of coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures (Ostwald ripening of solid domains in the liquid phase) was simulated using a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model. The simulation results were compared to experimental data previously obtained in a microgravity environment. Simulations were carried out as a function of the difference in chemical potential between Pb and Sn. Please the data layout document (DLD) describing the data organization in folders for each delta chemical potential and underlying files as per temperature of simulation and each time step.
_source.Hypothesis: Modified-embedded-atom (MEAM) interatomic potential and a one mode phase field crystal (1PFC) model can be utilized to simulate the kinetics of coarsening of solid phases in solid-liquid mixtures.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The proposed computational tool verified/quantified based on CSLM data will establish a virtual laboratory that can be used to study coarsening as well as other material processing phenomena on Earth involving with solid-liquid coexistence; e.g., rapid solidification and grain growth. Since computational models are highly repeatable at lower cost, the proposed modeling framework will result in accelerated material process development and certification. Solid-liquid coexistence is the initial step in many manufacturing technologies such as casting, liquid infiltration, and additive manufacturing. Hence, this modeling framework can be used to investigate the relations between these manufacturing processes and the material properties in order to optimize/control the manufacturing processes parameters. In addition, the results of this research will be disseminated to the public in forms of peer-reviewed articles, scientific reports, a project-specific website, and data uploaded to NASA-PSI website.

_source.Title: Testing Analytical and Numerical Models in Phase Coarsening using NASA Physical Sciences Informatics System
_source.Keywords: Simulations     Coarsening     Ostwald ripening     particle size distribution     multiparticle diffusion     PSD     2-D     CSLM
_source.Objectives:
NASA has supported “coarsening in solid–liquid mixtures” (CSLM) experiments, performed in microgravity on the International Space Station (ISS), with greatly reduced sedimentation rate in partially molten alloys. CSLM experimental data are stored in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI). Microgravity experiments offer a unique opportunity to test existing numerical modeling and theories of phase coarsening.

The objective of this research is to test existing numerical modeling methods for simulation of the microstructure evolution that occurs during phase coarsening, using experimental data for Sn-Pb mixtures currently held in PSI.

Results from this research can be found in the following publications:
Wang, K.G., Glicksman, M.E. Testing Numerical Modeling of Phase Coarsening by Microgravity Experiments. JOM 69, 2825–2830 (2017). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11837-017-2553-x
_source.Approach: (1) use data archived in NASA's PSI system from the Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures (CSLM) microgravity experiments to determine mean and maximum particle sizes in each sample processed through the CSLM microgravity experiments; (2) apply a two-dimensional (2-D) phase-field simulation code to allow simulation and evolution of initial microstructures that were observed in the CSLM experiments for Sn-Pb solid-liquid phase mixtures, and which provide input data for our phase-field code to numerically evolve coarsened microstructures over time; (3) calculate particle size distributions (PSDs) from the prior NASA CSLM experiments, our phase-field and multiparticle diffusion simulations, and from diffusion screening theory.
_source.Hypothesis: Phase-field and multiparticle diffusion numerical methods can be applied to simulate the evolution of the microstructure during phase coarsening, delivering accurate statistical physical quantities such as the particle size distribution (PSD). Phase-field modeling can adequately capture the complexity of the microstructures developed during phase coarsening at large volume fraction. In contrast, multiparticle diffusion modeling can track the evolution of microstructures consisting of nearly spherical particles that develop during phase coarsening at lower volume fraction.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The contributions from our research activities improved the understanding of fundamental materials phenomena, i.e., phase coarsening. We advanced the state of the art in both theory and simulation. Better understanding of two-phase microstructures will help engineers improve process designs in economically important areas, including liquid-phase sintering for the production of hard tool materials. The theory and simulation tools developed herein that are tested by microgravity experiments, will provide technical pointers for the improvement of important processes, microstructures, and materials properties. The improved knowledge of microstructure evolution in this project will have significant impact on alloy design and service-life strategies for alloy materials. The theory and simulation tools developed will provide guidance toward exploring the structure and properties of alloys. Finally, the theoretical and computational tools will save money and time for alloy modification.

_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI grant
_source.Objectives: The primary objectives for this PSI grant include establishing a deeper mechanistic understanding of nucleate boiling under low-gravity conditions by conducting high-fidelity numerical simulations that replicate the flight conditions of prior ISS-based boiling experiments, specifically MABE and NPBX. The investigation seeks to characterize key mechanisms governing bubble growth, waiting time, vapor spreading, coalescence, and detachment under variable gravity levels, degrees of wall superheat, and levels of liquid subcooling. Central to the objectives is quantifying how heat flux divides between nucleate boiling and natural convection modes, evaluating how the contact angle modulates wall adhesion forces, and determining the precise contribution of microlayer evaporation to heat transfer during low-gravity operation. By leveraging validated direct-numerical-simulation approaches tied to empirical MABE and NPBX measurements, this objective generates fundamental physics-based insights that enable predictive modeling of boiling processes relevant to spacecraft systems and advanced thermal architectures.
_source.Approach: The project approach was to use validated high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) ground-based computational simulations to numerically reproduce MABE- and NPBX-like boiling environments over a controlled range of heater temperatures, wall superheat conditions, and fluid subcooling levels. The research draws directly from ISS-acquired datasets that include detailed bubble growth dynamics, heat-flux profiles, and heater-surface imaging, which serve as reference benchmarks that guide simulation fidelity. Multiphase DNS simulations incorporate fluid phase-change physics, contact-line motion, interphase mass transport, and three-dimensional flow-field resolution to connect bubble behavior to instantaneous and time-averaged heat transfer. Iterative simulation campaigns then probe how variable gravitational acceleration, wettability contrast, bubble confinement, and microlayer evaporation influence overall heat-flux partitioning. The resulting database enables first-principles analysis of changes in boiling performance between terrestrial and microgravity settings while supporting quantitative model development applicable to spaceflight hardware, thermal architectures, and advanced electronic cooling systems.
_source.Hypothesis: The research was based on the hypothesis that, in microgravity, shifts in the relative influence of buoyancy, capillary forces, and microlayer evaporation fundamentally alter bubble-growth behavior and reduce heat-flux performance. It further hypothesized that these low-gravity effects can be accurately captured using high-fidelity Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS) validated against historic ISS boiling data from the MABE and NPBX experiments. By exploring variations in gravity, surface wettability, and thermal conditions, the study aimed to test the mechanisms governing bubble dynamics and heat transfer for application to spacecraft thermal management.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Space Benefits: This investigation provides high-resolution insight into how boiling heat-transfer efficiency degrades under reduced gravity, enabling the development of more reliable spacecraft thermal-management systems that do not depend solely on buoyancy-driven vapor removal. Improved understanding of microlayer-based transport, contact-line wetting, spatial heat-flux distribution, and boiling-mode transition directly supports the design of future ISS and deep-space thermal architectures, power-electronics packaging, life-support thermal management, and compact, energy-efficient cooling platforms for extended-duration missions.


Earth Benefits: The computational foundations and physics-based insights gained through this study directly advance terrestrial thermal-management strategies for high-power electronic systems, including server-class processors, power-dense computing architectures, and high-performance energy-conversion systems. The work improves predictive control of boiling-induced heat removal, enabling higher operating throughput, greater component longevity, and reduced power consumption in heat-intensive commercial and defense electronics.

_source.Keywords: Flame Spread     Fire suppression system     Damkohler number     Boundary layer     Fire safety     Forced Flow Flame     Kinetic regime
_source.Objectives:
The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow.
_source.Approach:
The experiment was conducted aboard the International Space Station (ISS) inside the Microgravity Glove Box (MSG). Custom-made fabric samples consisting of 75% cotton and 25% fiberglass (by mass) measuring were used as a fuel source as well as Nomex fabric and Ultem. A Kanthal wire (29-gage)igniter was used to initiate combustion at one end of the fabric. Airflow was controlled using a variable speed fan, with airflow speeds reaching as high as 40 cm/s. The airflow was directed along the fuel surface in either the opposed or concurrent direction.

This investigation explored two primary air flow configurations; concurrent-flow and opposed-flow. With concurrent-flow air flows in the same direction as the flame spread and in opposed-flow air flows in the opposite direction of flame spread. Flames were observed in the top and edge profiles and data was collected on flame size, shape, color, spread rate, and potential flame quenching. The samples were placed in a small flow duct (76 mm x 76 mm cross section) that allowed for airflow across the fabric. Other sample shapes were utilized as well including spheres and cylinders.
_source.Hypothesis: BASS experiments were based on the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions being identical (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature, etc.) To test this hypothesis with any but the thinnest materials requires extended microgravity time – longer than available in drop towers or parabolic aircraft.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.
BASS results provide essential guidance to ground-based microgravity combustion research efforts. Detailed combustion models are validated using the simpler flow environment afforded by tests in microgravity. Once validated, they can be used to build more complex combustion models needed to capture the important details of flames burning in normal gravity. These models have wide applicability to the general understanding of many terrestrial combustion problems and will guide novel spacecraft design and ensure the safety of future crewed missions.

_source.Title: Validation of a CFD Model for Gas-Liquid Flows in Packed Bed Reactors to Enable Thermo-Fluid Analysis in Microgravity
_source.Keywords: Validation of a CFD model     packed bed reactor
_source.Objectives:
1. Develop and validate computational models for gas-liquid two-phase flow in porous media under microgravity using the  PBRE (Packed Bed Reactor Experiment) flight data available in Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI).
2. Understand capillary-dominated fluid dynamics in low-gravity environments where traditional gravity-driven models fail.
3. Advance CFD tools to support the design and scale-up of life support and thermal control systems for spacecraft, space stations, and lunar/Martian habitats.
_source.Approach:
In this grant, our approach combined high-fidelity simulations with reduced-order modeling to better understand and predict two-phase gas-liquid flows through packed bed reactors in microgravity. We began by developing interface-resolved CFD simulations using the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method to capture detailed bubble dynamics in a representative volume of the reactor. These simulations were validated using PBRE imagery and pressure data available in PSI.

To address scale-up and improve computational efficiency, we also developed a two-fluid model (TFM), which treats the gas and liquid phases as interpenetrating continua rather than tracking individual interfaces. We calibrated the drag closure in this model using PBRE data, allowing us to predict pressure drop behavior across different flow regimes. By combining detailed CFD with a validated TFM, we created a versatile modeling framework that supports the design of life support and thermal systems for future space missions.

In space, fluid behavior becomes unpredictable. This grant developed and validated advanced computational models using real data from microgravity experiments to improve our understanding of how gas and liquid mixtures flow through packed bed reactors in space systems. This research can enable the design of more reliable and scalable systems for future missions to the Moon and Mars.

On Earth, the same fluid dynamics apply to industries like chemical processing, wastewater treatment, and energy systems. The resulting models and insights from this research can improve efficiency and reduce costs in these applications.

_source.Keywords: BCAT     transitions     Phase-field modeling     Hydrodynamic interactions
_source.Proposal Title: Phase Transitions in Colloid-Polymer Mixtures in Microgravity
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI grant
_source.Objectives: The objective of this PSI grant was to advance the understanding of phase transitions in colloid–polymer mixtures under microgravity conditions by integrating experimental observations with predictive modeling. Specifically, the research sought to determine how depletion interactions, arising from non-adsorbing polymers, influence the kinetics and morphology of phase separation and crystallization in complex fluids. By analyzing image data from NASA’s Binary Colloidal Alloy Test (BCAT-3 through BCAT-6) experiments conducted on the International Space Station, the project aimed to isolate the effects of gravity on phase behavior, quantify domain growth over multiple orders of magnitude in time and length scale, and develop a theoretical framework that connects these dynamics to hydrodynamic and thermodynamic parameters. Ultimately, this work sought to establish colloidal systems as model analogues for atomic and molecular phase transitions, providing insight relevant to both fundamental soft-matter physics and applied materials design.
_source.Approach: The approach combined data-driven analysis of PSI-archived BCAT imagery with a phase-field modeling framework that coupled the Cahn–Hilliard and Stokes equations to simulate phase separation in colloid–polymer mixtures. Experimental image sequences were processed for BCAT-3, -4 and -5, using algorithms in ImageJ and MATLAB to remove background noise, enhance contrast, and compute spatial autocorrelation functions for extracting characteristic domain length scales. Theoretical modeling of BCAT-5 incorporated concentration-dependent mobility and viscosity, along with Korteweg stresses to represent interfacial tension effects, allowing for the inclusion of hydrodynamic interactions that influenced domain coarsening. The governing equations were solved using a pseudospectral semi-implicit numerical scheme, and simulation results were quantitatively compared to flight data from the BCAT experiments. Model parameters were tuned using physical data from PSI to validate predictions and refine understanding of hydrodynamic coupling, phase-domain morphology, and kinetic arrest in colloid–polymer systems. This integrated experimental–theoretical approach yielded a comprehensive, microgravity-validated description of soft-matter phase transformation mechanisms.
_source.Hypothesis: Introducing non-adsorbing polymers into colloidal suspensions generates depletion-induced attractions that alter phase-transition kinetics; in microgravity, free from sedimentation and convection, these interactions can be directly modeled to reveal the intrinsic role of hydrodynamics in phase separation.

_source.Keywords: grant     scanning electron microscopy     micromechanics analysis code with generalized method of cells     micromechanics-based modeling     MICS     cement
_source.Proposal Title: Micromechanics-based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity
_source.Objectives:
Micromechanics‑Based Modeling of Cement Solidified in the Microgravity aimed to advance knowledge of the mechanical properties of cement binders formed in reduced gravity by leveraging microgravity materials data, such as SEM/BSE micrographs, available in the PSI database.
This project sought to connect microstructure (e.g., porosity, phase morphology such as portlandite) observed in ISS‑cured tricalcium silicate (C3S) pastes to bulk mechanical/transport behavior through modeling, thereby informing design and engineering of cementitious materials for extraterrestrial construction and providing validated simulation data that scale sparse flight samples to application‑relevant sizes.
_source.Approach:
In this work, the micromechanics analysis code with generalized method of cells (MAC/GMC) was used to predict the structure-property relationship of these unique cement samples.
First, the sparse data of cement hydrated in microgravity environment was converted to high-fidelity 3D microstructure with the aid of a deep learning-based microstructure methodology. The reconstructed sub-volumes were compared against micro-CT data using statistical descriptors. Second, the sub-volumes (partitioned based on individual constituents) of such reconstructed 3D structures were fed into the NASA Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to obtain homogenized properties of the cement. A semi-automated Python script was developed to complete the workflow.  Owing to the high computational demand, the analyses were carried out in NASA Advanced Supercomputing (NAS) servers.

Phase‑discerned ISS and ground BSE/SEM images were segmented and reconstructed into 3D volumes using a deep learning microstructure framework; these Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) were then analyzed with NASA’s Multiscale Analysis Tool (NASMAT) to homogenize and predict effective properties. Reconstruction quality was validated against statistical descriptors and micro‑CT data, and the modeling spans length‑scale partitioning to capture porous, multiphase behavior.
The experimental basis originated from the MICS investigation (PSI‑84 in the database), which conducted controlled ISS/ground hydration in sealed Burst Pouches, keeping temperature/pressure/humidity constant so gravity is the sole variable, followed by porosimetry, TGA, XRD, EDS/EMPA, and image analysis to quantify phase fractions and pore structures that feed the modeling pipeline.
_source.Hypothesis: Consistent with the microgravity MICS investigation, the central hypothesis was that minimizing gravity‑driven transport (buoyancy, sedimentation, convection) yields a diffusion‑controlled hydration process in microgravity, producing more uniform phase distributions and distinct microstructures (e.g., higher porosity, altered portlandite morphology) relative to 1g; these differences are expected to translate into measurably different mechanical properties for µg‑hardened cement paste versus terrestrial cement. The grant tested this by quantifying microstructural features from flight/ground samples and propagating them through micromechanics to predict property deltas attributable to gravity effects.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
This research provides the first reference simulation data and a practical route to predict how cement (including regolith‑based mixes) behaves when fabricated in space, which can inform Artemis‑aligned or other space-based habitat concepts and construction logistics where transporting bulk materials is prohibitive.
On Earth, the deep-learning-assisted reconstruction and micromechanics workflow developed can be applied to other multiphase materials, enabling materials-by-design even when only a limited samples are available. By clarifying how processing conditions in microgravity affect cement structure and performance, such as the ~70% porosity and plate-like portlandite observed in ISS samples, this work improves predictive models for optimizing mix designs and curing conditions in constrained environments. These advances also benefit low-resource or extreme-environment construction on Earth and contribute more broadly to the ICME community.

_source.Title: Cold Atom Lab - Fundamental Interactions for Atom Interferometry with Ultracold Quantum Gases in a Microgravity Environment
_source.Keywords: Bose-Einstein Condensates     Atom Interferometry     Precision Quantum Metrology     Feshbach Molecules
_source.Objectives: Precision atom interferometers (AI) in space promise exciting technical capabilities with diverse applications of interest to NASA. These quantum sensors are particularly relevant for fundamental physics research, with proposals including unprecedented tests of the validity of the weak equivalence principle, precision measurements of the fine structure and gravitational constants, and detection of gravity waves and dark matter/dark energy. This investigation will utilize the capabilities of NASA's multi-user Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL), in the microgravity environment onboard the International Space Station (ISS), to study mitigation schemes for the leading-order systematics expected to limit future high-precision measurements of fundamental physics with AIs in microgravity. The flight experiments, supported by theoretical investigations and ground studies at Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), will concentrate on the physics of pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics in ultracold quantum gases as a means to overcome uncontrolled AI shifts associated with the gravity gradient and few-particle collisions. A space-based dual-species AI will be further developed and used, which is planned as an on-orbit upgrade to the CAL science module after approximately a year of science investigations, for proof-of-principle tests of systematic mitigations and phase-readout techniques for use in the next-generation of precision metrology experiments based on AIs in microgravity. The proposed studies require the effective position invariance, long free fall times, and extremely low temperature samples uniquely available with the CAL apparatus. It is anticipated that these studies can lead to the unprecedented level of control and accuracy necessary for AIs to explore some of the most fundamental physical concepts in nature.
_source.Approach:
Investigation comprises two main aspects: the creation of ultracold atomic gases and the subsequent manipulation and probing of these gases to study systematic mitigations. For dual-species operations the process is slightly more complicated, especially with the addition of a sympathetic cooling step, however, the general process is fairly standardized.

Creation of Ultracold Atomic Gas:

   -Laser Cooling: Atoms are released into a vacuum chamber and collected into a magneto-optical trap (MOT), where they are initially cooled using laser cooling techniques. This technique cools the sample by
   essentially ‘pushing’ the laser against the motion of the atoms effectively lowering the momentum, and therefore the velocity, kinetic energy, and temperature, of the sample. This is followed by brief stages of
   “compressed MOT”, in which the trapping force of the MOT is increased to compress the gas, and then an “optical molasses” stage, during which the quadrupole magnetic field is turned off and the laser
   frequency is further detuned to minimize the temperature of the gases.

   -State Preparation: The sample is optically pumped to a low magnetic field-seeking quantum state. The atoms in this state are then subjected to an intermediate quadrupole magnetic field which traps the
   atoms from the MOT and allows for the transfer from the MOT, located at the bottom of the science region, to an atom-chip-based trap, located at the top of the science region.

   -Evaporative Cooling: The atoms undergo forced evaporative cooling, using frequency sweeps of either RF or microwave fields, to bring the gases below the critical temperature, leading to the formation of a
   Bose-Einstein Condensate (BEC). Evaporative cooling cools the sample by removing the highest-energy atom from the trap so that the remaining atoms re-thermalize at progressively lower temperatures.

   -Decompression and Release: The tightness of the atom trap is adiabatically relaxed to further cool the atoms via decompression colling. After a short hold time in the relaxed trap, the atoms are released by
   rapidly turning the atom-chip and bias coil currents to zero to allow the atoms to expand in freefall. At this point, investigators can search for the primary signatures of a BECs for confirmation that one was
   formed. Formation of a BEC is typically associated with the behavior of the velocity distribution, such as the presence of a narrow peak centered at near zero velocity and the low velocity peak growing
   (greater fraction of atoms in this domain) as the temperature decreases.

Manipulation and Probing:

   -Probing Techniques: The ultracold gas is probed in freefall using laser, magnetic field, radiofrequency, and/or microwave pulses. These techniques are designed to establish atoms in the proper state,
    perform atom interferometry, or establish and investigate the pairwise interactions and molecular dynamics crucial for mitigating systematics in high-precision measurements.

   -Time-of-Flight Imaging: After a predetermined time of flight, the sample is imaged using absorption imaging techniques. This process involves shining resonant light on the atoms and taking two images, per
   atomic species, of the shadow cast in the light: one of the sample and a reference image post-destruction of the sample. As implied, this is the end of the experimental cycle for this specific BEC as the
   measurement process destroys the sample.

This approach is particularly suited for studying mitigation schemes for leading-order systematics that can affect future high-precision measurements with atom interferometers (AIs) in microgravity. By leveraging the unique microgravity environment provided by NASA’s Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL) on the International Space Station, this investigation aims to achieve the level of control and accuracy required for groundbreaking tests of fundamental physics principles, such as the weak equivalence principle, and precision measurements of the fine structure and gravitational constants. The integration of theoretical investigations and ground studies at JPL supports these flight experiments, enabling comprehensive understanding and development of systematic mitigation techniques.
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that the control of interactions and association/dissociation of weakly-bound molecules in ultracold quantum gases can overcome uncontrolled Atomic Interference (AI) shifts in space which are caused by the gravity gradient and few-particle collisions. Investigators will interrogate this hypothesis by conducting tests using ultracold quantum gases and exploring Feshbach resonances at new energy regimes.  Investigators expect unprecedented levels of control and accuracy in the AI that will enable exploration of some of the most fundamental physical concepts in nature and open up venues for exploration of novel quantum phases in exotic dynamical regimes.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Our studies are designed to achieve technological advances in precision metrology that can only be realized in the microgravity environment of the Cold Atom Laboratory (CAL).  The tools of ultracold atomic and molecular physics are utilized (namely Feshbach resonances) for exquisite control of the differential center-of-mass distributions of the dual-species quantum gases and on methods to use the fundamentals of few-body interactions to maintain coherence in atomic ensembles for enhanced precision sensor capabilities. Subsequent proof-of-principle studies with the dual-species atom interferometer on CAL will further advance the state of the art for precision interferometry with ultracold matter waves. The impact of such research to the field of metrology can be seen through its potential to increase precision for atom-interferometry and also the possibility of engineering highly efficient system-specific devices based on the fundamental nature of few-body interactions. The microgravity environment of the CAL facility strongly favors such explorations and allow for the possibility of uncovering novel effects and quantum phases of matter, a major goal in ultracold quantum gases and other disciplines of fundamental physics. These studies can benefit life on Earth by providing both fundamental understanding of nature in previously inaccessible environments and energy regimes, and by enhancing the tools available for scientific exploration at the highest precision.

_source.Keywords: fuel dilution     Diffusion Flame     inlet velocity     Fuels
_source.Objectives:
Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

Specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.
_source.Approach: The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions. A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images. Calibration tests for airflow velocity, soot measurement, and the fans were conducted to ensure the accuracy of the results. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments. Data was then analyzed to correlate flame structure with stability with flow dynamics and fuel properties.
_source.Hypothesis: The hypothesis is that the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity are significantly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel composition and are fundamentally different than flames observed on Earth.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
1. Improved numerical models for flame behavior lead to more efficient combustion technologies on Earth.
2. Understanding soot formation aids in designing combustion systems with minimum emissions.
3. Insights into flame stability and behavior to enhance fire safety.
4. Findings will inform the development of cleaner, more efficient engines and industrial burners.

_source.Proposal Title: Characterization of Smoke from Microgravity Fires for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection
_source.Objectives:
The objectives of this investigation were to:
(1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal
gravity material flammability screening test.
_source.Approach: The Saffire-1 experiments was performed on the Orbital Science’s Cygnus resupply vehicle after it deberthed from the ISS. The sample material for Saffire-I is a composite fabric called Sibal consisting of cotton on a fiberglass substrate (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass by weight). It has been used in many space experiments because it burns like cotton but maintains structural integrity after the cotton is consumed. The sample was approximately 0.94 meters long and 0.4 meters wide, simulating a large piece of flammable fabric. The Saffire-1 flight unit had a sample card installed in the middle of a large flow duct. Air is drawn through the flow duct by fans located at the top of the duct with flow straighteners at the bottom of the experiment module. Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s. Once the sample was ignited flame images were captured using two cameras. In addition, thermocouples provided flow, flame, and plume temperatures, two radiometers recorded flame radiation, solid state sensors were used to measure pressure, CO2 and O2 mole faction, and two anemometer tracked flow velocity. All data was compressed, and subsequently downlinked.
_source.Hypothesis: This investigation hypothesizes that due to large differences between fire behavior in normal and reduced gravity, the use of terrestrial fires and fire standards to design spacecraft fire safety systems presents an inherent risk to the vehicle because of the significant level of uncertainty. While this approach has been successful thus far, the uncertainty and risk will increase as exploration missions venture further from earth with considerably longer transit times for a safe return. There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures. To address this knowledge gap, this investigation proposed to conduct large-scale fire safety experiments in an expendable spacecraft without risk to a crew.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The Saffire-I experiment provides a new way to study a realistic fire on an exploration vehicle, which has not been possible in the past because the risks are too high. Instruments on an unmanned cargo vessel measure oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure and flame growth, and two video cameras provide views of the flame. Results determine microgravity flammability limits for several spacecraft materials, help to validate NASA’s material selection criteria, and how microgravity and limited oxygen affect flame size. The investigation is crucial for the safety of current and future space missions. Studying fire in small, sealed environments such as the Cygnus cargo supply vehicle benefits fire safety and prevention efforts on Earth, including inside mines, airplanes, or submarines.

_source.Title: Investigating the Structures of Paramagnetic Aggregates from Colloidal Emulsions-2
_source.Keywords: Colloids     magnetorheological (MR) fluid     self-assembly     microgravity     pulsed fields     buckling
_source.Objectives:
InSPACE-2 studied the kinetics of chain formation in DC fields for suspensions of monodisperse, super-paramagnetic colloidal microspheres.  Objectives included:
1) To understand the percolation transition of MR suspensions in microgravity and the behavior of structures around this point (incipient structure).  The fluctuations of these chains can also be used to estimate the microrheological response of the MR fluid.  Additionally, measurements of the chain fluctuations in the final gelled material provide an estimate of the storage modulus of the suspension.
2) To determine the lowest energy configuration of 3D particle structures formed in a magnetorheological (MR) fluid in a pulsed magnetic field. Visual observations of microscopic structures will yield a better understanding of the interplay of the forces and interactions (magnetizing/demagnetizing, surface energy, and repulsion between structures) in MR suspensions. The most important dipolar interactions are the demagnetizing field, surface energy, and repulsion between structures.
_source.Approach: InSPACE-2 employed a microscopic video technique to study the internal microstructure in MR fluid suspensions. The investigation studied the assembly of magnetic particles in the presence of a toggled magnetic field. The microstructure of the suspension as the particles assemble was characterized by light microscopy. Samples for InSPACE-2 consisted of 1.05 μm diameter colloidal particles suspended in an aqueous phase. The particles were Dynabeads MyOne Carboxylic Acid from Invitrogen at four different concentrations, 0.40, 0.48, 0.56, 0.65%. When exposed to a continuous magnetic field each particle in the fluid acquires a magnetic dipole moment. Such dipoles mutually interact and align to form a particle chain structures. At sufficient concentrations and field strengths these chains form columns that cross-link to form an interconnected network.  The effects of sedimentation, which prohibits maintaining the particle concentration uniformity throughout the fluid, affect the study of MR fluids. Mechanical properties of the particle assemblies, especially buckling instabilities, will be characterized.
_source.Hypothesis: The primary hypothesis is that energy barriers preventing colloidal phase transition can be overcome by changing the magnetic driving frequency and forces. In these gel systems, gravity plays a dominant role and would slowly compress and deform the gel structures when similar experiments are performed on Earth, whereas in space these structures can be maintained as long as the magnetic forces are applied.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The MR fluids studied in InSPACE-2 are a unique model system for studying the fundamental mechanisms of phase transitions and self-assembly. Suspension phase behavior affects the processing, stability and final properties of foods, personal care products, agrochemicals, paints, inks, pharmaceuticals and numerous other products and materials in which fine particles are suspended in fluids. Additionally, InSPACE-2 research emphasizes how to harness external fields in order to direct the assembly of novel micro- and nano-structured materials and devices. Such field-directed self-assembly represents a bottom-up approach to material and device fabrication, with the potential to dramatically reduce the cost of advanced technologies in photonics, heat transfer and photovoltaics. The MR response provides the basis for technologies ranging from actively controlled dampers and actuators to magnetically sealed bearings and sensitive stress transducers. MR fluids are currently used in wide range of applications, including active automotive shock absorbers, and engineers have explored their use in seismic dampers to protect large-scale structures during violent earthquakes. Applications for space exploration include their potential use in robots, rovers, and for mobility augmentation crew suits. Understanding the microstructural evolution of MR suspensions under time-varying conditions provides critical information for engineering and for tailoring their mechanical behavior.

_source.Title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
_source.Keywords: Cool Flames     thermo-convective perturbation     Droplet combustion     FLEX
_source.Proposal Title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
_source.Sponsoring Agency: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)  PSI grant
_source.Objectives: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.
_source.Approach:
OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.
_source.Hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits:
Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials.
Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

_source.Title: Coarsening in Solid-Liquid Mixtures
_source.Keywords: Microgravity     Dendritic structure     dendritic arm     Interfacial Shape Distribution     Phase Field Modeling
_source.Objectives: The objective of this investigation was to study dendritic coarsening in solid-liquid mixtures at low volume fractions of solid. Specific interest was in examining dendritic structure close to the dendrite tip. Additional objectives included measuring the rate at which topological singularities  occur when a secondary dendrite arm separates from the main dendrite stem or when two arms fuse together.
_source.Approach: The CSLM-3 approach and hardware was essentially identical to the predecessor CSLM and CSLM-2 investigations. The solid volume fraction of the 4 Pb-Sn samples for CSLM-3 were 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4. Isothermal holding times between 10 minutes and 48 hours were employed. After the requisite holding times the samples were quenched using pressurized gas. Upon receipt of the samples they were analyzed using three-dimensional reconstructions of the microstructure. The 3D reconstructions was used to determine the interfacial curvatures, the genus and the spatial distribution of curvature in the system. The experimentally measured structures were used to compare phase field simulations and experiment.
_source.Hypothesis:
The fundamental questions that this investigation attempts to answer are as follows:
Does the Interface Shape Distribution (ISD) vary with position from the tip of the dendrite? If so, as is likely the case, does the ISD scale with time, as is usually the case during coarsening? How important is the spatial distribution of curvature in setting the evolution of the structure? How do diffusional interactions between the secondary, and perhaps tertiary, arms on different dendrites affect the evolution of the system? How does the ISD evolve when there are multiple dendrites in the system? Does scaling exist?
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: Coarsening occurs on Earth during the processing of any metal alloy and thus the coarsening process affects a large spectrum of products from dental fillings to turbine blades. Since the properties of an alloy are linked to the size of the particles within the solid, coarsening can be used to strengthen materials. This is the case with the majority of aluminum alloys used commercially today. Conversely, if the coarsening process proceeds too long the material can weaken. This occurs in jet turbine blades and is one of the reasons why turbine blades must be replaced after a certain number of hours of service. This investigation will provide insights into the dynamics of dendritic morphological evolution and will point the way to the formulation of models of this technologically important coarsening process. Thus developing accurate models of the coarsening process and validating them using benchmark experimental data is central to creating a wide range of new materials encompassing those used in automobiles to those used in space applications.

_source.Title: Development and Verification of a 3D Nucleate Pool Boiling Simulation Model Using PSI Data
_source.Keywords: PSI Grant     numerical method     heat transfer rate     moment-of-fluid (MOF) procedure     multi-material systems     complex boundaries     discontinuous diffusion coefficients
_source.Objectives: The primary objective of this investigation was to develop and validate a numerical model for further investigation of nucleate pool boiling problems under microgravity conditions.
_source.Approach:
The moment-of-fluid (MOF) procedure is employed to reconstruct the interfaces of any number of material interfaces in a computational cell. The salient features of the overall approach includes:
(i) Multi-material interfaces are represented by the piecewise linear moment-of-fluid (MOF) reconstruction, (ii)  the time derivative part of the heat equation is discretized using the backward Euler method which is a discrete maximum principle preserving time discretization scheme, (iii) the spatial derivatives part of the heat equation is discretized using the finite volume method, (iv) the temperature field is discretized on a multi-material “supermesh” in which there is just one temperature variable per material per cell, (v) the discrete location for a given variable is at the materials' centroid, (vi) “connected centroid” method is used in order to approximate fluxes, (vii) at Dirichlet or Neumann embedded interfaces,  a linear exact correction term is prescribed so that the method approximates the temperature gradient with second order accuracy.
_source.Hypothesis: It is hypothesized that the developed model will have the following advantages which can lead to a more accurate prediction: (1) the method can better resolve thermal boundary layers (away from triple points) using adaptive mesh refinement, (2) a novel Moment of Fluid multiphase flow algorithm will  straightforwardly prescribe a microlayer model in 3D general geometries, (3) the moment of fluid interface capturing algorithm will enable better handling of 3D problems such as bubble merging, (4) the modeling method can better conserve the boiling mass flow rate by directly exploiting the moment-of-fluid (sharp) interface reconstruction for approximating the interface heat flux in the vicinity of multiple (greater than 2) materials.
_source.Research Impacts/Earth Benefits: The verified model can be used to further study scenarios not investigated on ISS such as vapor bubble departure and collapse. It can also be used to identify optimal heated surface configuration for better heat transfer characteristics. In addition, the model can be used to study other problems under microgravity such as packed bed reactors. The development of nucleate pool boiling simulation tool in microgravity based on the Navier-Stokes equations from this proposed work can be used to study other boiling problems in Earth gravity such as engine cooling and cooling in electronic devices.
